title: Qatar | AML/CFT Compliance under Law No. 20 of 2019 and QCB Instructions
tagline: Qatar's AML/CFT law and QCB Instructions in practice: CDD, PEPs, wires, sanctions screening, STRs to the QFIU and your bank's programme.
sectors: Conventional banks licensed by the Qatar Central Bank
Payments, money transfers and correspondent banking
description:
A country-specific quest for staff of **conventional banks licensed and supervised by the Qatar Central Bank (QCB)** outside the Qatar Financial Centre. It is built on **Law No. 20 of 2019 on Combating Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing** (amended by Decree-Law No. 19 of 2021), the **QCB Anti-Money Laundering and Combating Terrorism Financing Instructions for Financial Institutions (May 2020 edition)** and the **QFIU's Instructions on Implementing Suspicious Transactions Reporting Requirements (April 2024)**, with targeted financial sanctions covered in general terms.

The QCB Instructions make an ongoing AML/CFT training programme part of every bank's AML/CFT programme and require all officers and employees to be trained at least once a year and whenever needed, so this quest is for everyone from tellers to board members. You will learn the offences, the risk-based approach, CDD, beneficial ownership and PEP rules, wire transfer and correspondent banking duties, screening against UN and NCTC lists, how and when to report to the QFIU without tipping off, ten-year record keeping and what the QCB expects of your institution's programme.

Penalty amounts are not quoted (the 2021 amendment is in Arabic only). QFC firms follow the QFCRA's separate rules.

This quest builds knowledge of Qatar's framework; it does not replace your institution's own AML/CFT policies and procedures, which you must always follow.
audience: All employees of QCB-licensed conventional banks who need annual AML/CFT training or a refresher
Branch, money transfer and relationship staff who onboard customers and handle cash and payments
Onboarding, KYC, screening and transaction monitoring teams applying CDD, EDD and sanctions checks
Payments, trade finance and correspondent banking staff handling cross-border flows
MLROs, Deputy MLROs, internal auditors, senior managers and board members accountable for the programme
outcomes: Explain Qatar's AML/CFT framework, the ML and TF offences and the roles of the QCB, QFIU, national committee and NCTC
Apply the risk-based approach, CDD triggers, the 20% beneficial ownership test and PEP rules in the QCB Instructions
Handle ongoing monitoring, wire transfer information, correspondent relationships and sanctions list matches correctly
Escalate suspicion to the MLRO, meet the QFIU's reporting deadlines and avoid tipping off
Describe the board's and MLRO's duties, annual training, ten-year record keeping, audit and supervisory measures

quest.name: Guardians of the Pearl Gate
quest.premise: You have just joined the AML/CFT Department of Dafna Bank, a fictional conventional bank licensed by the Qatar Central Bank, with its head office in West Bay, Doha, and branches in Al Wakrah and Al Khor. The QCB has asked for the bank's annual AML/CFT review and training evidence. With MLRO Noora Al Kuwari, branch manager Faisal Al Mannai, analyst Anjali Menon and payments manager Samuel Owusu, clear five stages, then face the final boss: briefing chief executive Hamad Al Sulaiti and the board.

badge.name: Qatar AML Guardian
badge.description: Awarded to bank staff who can apply Qatar's AML/CFT law and QCB Instructions: know the customer, report to the QFIU on time and run a sound programme.

sessions.title: Qatar's AML/CFT Framework: Law No. 20 of 2019, the Offences and Who Does What
sessions.summary: Map Qatar's AML/CFT rulebook: Law No. 20 of 2019 and its Implementing Regulations, the QCB AML/CFT Instructions of May 2020, the QFIU's reporting instructions, the money laundering and terrorist financing offences, and the authorities you will deal with.
objectives: Describe the layers of Qatar's AML/CFT framework from Law No. 20 of 2019 down to your bank's own procedures
Explain the money laundering and terrorist financing offences and what makes them broad
Name the roles of the QCB, the QFIU, the national AML/CFT committee, the NCTC and the Public Prosecution
Recognise that bank staff can face personal criminal and supervisory consequences for breaching AML/CFT duties

cards.title: Day one at Dafna Bank
cards.setting: AML/CFT Department, Dafna Bank head office, West Bay, Doha. 8:30 am, Sunday.

lines.text: Your new badge opens the glass door of the AML/CFT Department. On your desk sits a printed copy of the bank's AML/CFT policy, already covered in sticky notes.
Welcome to Dafna Bank. I'm Noora, the bank's MLRO. You picked a lively week to join us.
Qatar Central Bank has asked for our annual AML/CFT policy review and training records, and our yearly training cycle starts now. You're going to help me run it.
(on a video call from the Al Wakrah branch) Faisal here. One of my tellers asked me a fair question: if the police deal with criminals, why do we fill in so many forms?
And my monitoring team keeps asking which rules come from the law and which come from QCB. Our procedures mix them up.
Then the first stage is the Pearl Gate: the map of the whole framework. Once you see the layers, every form makes sense.
Ready? By lunchtime you should be able to answer Faisal's teller yourself.

cards.title: Qatar's AML/CFT framework in five scenes

scenes.heading: The law at the top
scenes.narration: Law Number 20 of 2019 is Qatar's anti-money laundering and terrorist financing law. It replaced the 2010 law, defines the offences, sets the duties of banks and creates the key authorities. It was amended in 2021.

scenes.heading: The regulations underneath
scenes.narration: A Council of Ministers decision issued the law's Implementing Regulations in 2019. They add detail to the duties the law sets out.

scenes.heading: Your supervisor's rulebook
scenes.narration: Qatar Central Bank supervises banks outside the Qatar Financial Centre. Its AML/CFT Instructions for financial institutions, May 2020 edition, turn the law into day-to-day rules for banks.

scenes.heading: Where suspicions go
scenes.narration: The Qatar Financial Information Unit, the QFIU, is the national centre that receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports. In April 2024 it issued binding instructions on how to report.

scenes.heading: Separate lanes
scenes.narration: Terrorist designations are circulated by the National Counter Terrorism Committee. Firms in the Qatar Financial Centre follow their own regulator, the QFCRA, and are outside this quest.

cards.title: Layers of Qatar's AML/CFT rulebook
cards.caption: Each layer must be consistent with the one above it. When they differ, the higher layer wins, and your bank's procedures must be updated.

items.label: Implementing Regulations

items.label: Dafna Bank policies

cards.title: Who does what in Qatar
cards.prompt: Match each authority with its main AML/CFT role.

pairs.right: Licenses and supervises banks, issues the AML/CFT Instructions and imposes supervisory measures
Receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports and passes results to competent authorities
Runs the National Risk Assessment and the national strategy and coordinates the authorities
Circulates terrorist designations that banks must screen against
Investigates and prosecutes money laundering and terrorist financing offences
Supervises firms in the Qatar Financial Centre under its own separate rules

cards.question: A teller at Dafna Bank has a suspicion about a customer. Under Qatar's framework, which body ultimately receives the bank's suspicious transaction report?
options: The Qatar Financial Information Unit, through the bank's MLRO
The Qatar Central Bank's AML/CFT supervision department
The Public Prosecution, directly from the teller
The National Counter Terrorism Committee
cards.explanation: Law No. 20 of 2019 makes the QFIU the national centre for receiving STRs, and the QCB Instructions require the MLRO or Deputy MLRO to file them. The QCB supervises the bank and may need to be informed in some cases, but it is not where STRs are filed.

cards.title: The money laundering offence under Article 2
Money laundering or terrorist financing?
cards.prompt: Place each situation in the offence it most closely describes under Law No. 20 of 2019.

items.text: A trader buys a villa with cash he knows came from a fraud
A donor collects legitimate salary savings to pay a fighter's travel to a conflict zone
A manager splits embezzled funds across relatives' accounts to hide them
A shop owner sends money to a designated terrorist group, with no specific attack planned
An accountant knowingly invoices fake services so bribe money looks like fees
A group raises small online donations to buy equipment for an attack
A person keeps a car bought for him with drug proceeds, knowing where the money came from

cards.title: The cousin's business
cards.setting: Al Wakrah branch, teller counter, 11:10 am.

lines.text: Noora, quick one. A customer just deposited QR 40,000 in cash and said it's his cousin's business money. He doesn't know what the business does.
That's an ML question. But here's mine: if the money is clean, say salary savings, can it still be terrorist financing?
Anjali has spotted the key difference. Money laundering is about where the money came from. Terrorist financing is about where it's going.
Under the law, TF covers funds from any source, legitimate or not, and it doesn't need a link to a specific attack.
So my tellers need to watch the purpose of a payment, not just its source?
Exactly. Let's flip through the TF offence so they know what to look for.

cards.front: Does the money have to be dirty?
cards.back: No. The TF offence covers funds from legitimate or illegitimate sources.

cards.front: Must the funds be linked to a specific attack?
cards.back: No. Funding an individual terrorist or a terrorist organisation is enough, even without a link to a particular act.

cards.front: Is paying for travel covered?
cards.back: Yes. Financing someone's travel to another country to commit, plan or train for terrorist acts is TF.

cards.front: Does location matter?
cards.back: No. The offence applies wherever the funder, the terrorist or the planned act is located.

cards.front: Must the money actually be used?
cards.back: No. The offence is committed even if the funds were never used for a terrorist act.

cards.front: How does TF connect to ML?
cards.back: TF is itself a predicate offence for money laundering, so dealing with TF funds can also be laundering.

cards.title: Two routes when things go wrong
cards.caption: Law No. 20 of 2019 provides both. The QCB Instructions say breaches are sanctioned under the law (they point to Article 44) and the QCB Law.

items.label: Typical trigger
items.left: A criminal offence, such as laundering, tipping off or failing to report
items.right: Breach of the law, regulations or QCB AML/CFT Instructions

items.label: Who can be targeted
items.left: Individuals and the bank as a legal person
items.right: The bank and its directors, board members and managers

items.label: Possible outcomes
items.right: Warnings, orders, fines, removal of managers, licence suspension or withdrawal

cards.title: The target-driven shortcut
cards.situation: Omar, a relationship manager at another branch, is under pressure to hit his account-opening target. A trading company's file is missing its ownership chart, and the director says the owners 'prefer privacy'. Omar asks you to approve the account today and collect the ownership details 'later, when things calm down'. What do you do?

choices.text: Approve it, because collecting documents later is common practice
choices.outcome: The account opens with unknown owners. If the company is later linked to crime, the bank has breached its CDD duties, and the law makes such breaches by staff an offence even through gross negligence, not only deliberate wrongdoing.

choices.text: Refuse to open the account until the owners are identified and verified, and tell Omar why
choices.outcome: Right. The law bars banks from starting a relationship when CDD cannot be completed. You protect the bank and Omar, and if the customer's refusal itself looks suspicious, you raise an internal STR with the MLRO.

choices.text: Open it with a restriction on outgoing payments until the chart arrives
choices.outcome: Better than nothing, but it still starts a relationship before the beneficial owners are identified. Delayed verification is allowed only in narrow, low-risk cases set by policy, and a customer refusing to name owners is not one.

cards.title: Real case: a car import that did not add up (QFIU, 2019)
cards.body:
At the QFIU's 2019 typologies workshop, a Qatari bank shared an anonymised case.

A company asked for a **letter of credit** to import new and used cars worth about **QR 23 million**. The beneficiary was in one neighbouring Gulf country, but the goods were loaded in another Middle Eastern country. When staff checked the detailed invoice, every car was priced **far below market value**, and the importer was not the authorised dealer for that brand in Qatar.

**Why it matters:** under-invoicing is a classic **trade-based money laundering** method: value moves across borders hidden inside the price of goods.

**Lessons for you:**

- Compare prices and routes with what is normal for the trade.
- A mismatch between the beneficiary's location and the goods' origin deserves questions.
- Unusual pricing is a reason to escalate to the MLRO, not to approve faster.

cards.question: Which statement about the money laundering offence in Law No. 20 of 2019 is correct?
options: Only offences committed inside Qatar can be predicate offences for laundering
The offence requires a confession, because intent cannot be inferred from facts
A person who commits the predicate crime cannot also be punished for laundering
Funds can be proven to be proceeds of crime without anyone first being convicted of the predicate offence
cards.explanation: The law treats laundering as an independent crime: a predicate conviction is not needed, offences abroad count when they are crimes in both countries, knowledge can be inferred from objective circumstances, and the predicate offender can also be punished for laundering.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: Law No. 20 of 2019 (amended in 2021) sits at the top, followed by the 2019 Implementing Regulations and the QCB AML/CFT Instructions of May 2020.
The QFIU receives STRs; the QCB supervises banks; the national committee runs the National Risk Assessment; the NCTC circulates terrorist designations.
Money laundering is a separate crime: no predicate conviction is needed and knowledge can be inferred from facts.
Terrorist financing covers clean money too and needs no link to a specific attack.
Breaches can lead to criminal penalties for individuals and the bank, and supervisory measures from the QCB.

cards.prompt: Think of one form or check you complete in your daily work. Which layer of Qatar's framework does it come from, and what would go wrong if you skipped it?

quiz.question: Which law is the main AML/CFT law that Dafna Bank must apply today?
options: Law No. 4 of 2010, as updated in 2019
Law No. 13 of 2012 on the Qatar Central Bank only
Law No. 27 of 2019 on Combating Terrorism only
Law No. 20 of 2019, as amended in 2021
quiz.explanation: Law No. 20 of 2019 repealed Law No. 4 of 2010 and was amended by Decree-Law No. 19 of 2021. The QCB Law and the counter-terrorism law matter too, but neither is the main AML/CFT law.

quiz.question: A procedure manual still quotes the QCB's 2010 AML/CFT regulations for financial institutions. What is the best assessment?
options: It needs updating, because the May 2020 Instructions replaced all earlier AML/CFT instructions
It is fine, because the 2010 regulations still apply alongside the 2020 Instructions for older procedures
It needs updating only if the QFIU rejects one of the bank's reports
It is fine, because procedures do not need to cite any regulatory source
quiz.explanation: The QCB Instructions state that all earlier AML/CFT instructions to financial institutions, including the June 2010 regulations, are cancelled and replaced. Waiting for a QFIU rejection confuses the reporting channel with the supervisor's rulebook.

quiz.question: Faisal's customer says the cash he deposits is from a cousin's business, but cannot say what the business does. For money laundering, what matters most?
options: Whether the cousin has already been convicted of a crime
Whether there is reason to suspect the funds are proceeds of a crime
Whether the amount is above a reporting threshold
Whether the customer is a Qatari national or a resident
quiz.explanation: Laundering concerns the criminal origin of funds. No predicate conviction is required and there is no monetary threshold for reporting suspicion, so the right question is whether there are grounds to suspect criminal proceeds.

quiz.question: A customer uses his clean salary savings to pay for a friend's flight abroad to join a terrorist training camp. How does Law No. 20 of 2019 treat this?
options: It is not an offence, because the money came from a lawful salary and no attack was ever carried out
It is money laundering, because the funds crossed a border
It is terrorist financing, because funding travel for terrorist training is covered whatever the source
It is an offence only if an attack later takes place
quiz.explanation: Article 3 covers funds from any source, includes financing travel for terrorist purposes or training, and does not depend on an attack happening. Laundering is about hiding criminal proceeds, which is not the issue here.

quiz.question: Which authority receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports in Qatar?
options: The Qatar Central Bank's supervision department
The National Counter Terrorism Committee
The Qatar Financial Centre Regulatory Authority
The Qatar Financial Information Unit (QFIU)
quiz.explanation: The law makes the QFIU, an operationally independent unit, the national centre for receiving and analysing STRs. The QCB supervises banks and the NCTC deals with terrorist designations.

quiz.question: Which body leads Qatar's National Risk Assessment of money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing under the 2019 law?
options: The National Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing Committee
The Qatar Financial Information Unit, through its strategic analysis department
Each bank's board of directors
The Qatar Financial Markets Authority
quiz.explanation: The law gives the national committee the task of preparing, documenting and updating the National Risk Assessment and the national strategy. Banks must take its results into account, but they do not run it, and the QFIU's role is financial intelligence.

quiz.question: A prosecutor argues that a defendant must have known the funds were criminal because he moved them through five accounts in two days for no business reason. Which rule supports this argument?
options: Knowledge must always be proven by a written confession
Knowledge and intent may be inferred from objective factual circumstances
Intent is irrelevant once funds move between accounts
Only bank staff who handled the transfers can give evidence about a customer's intent
quiz.explanation: Article 5 of Law No. 20 of 2019 allows knowledge and intent to be inferred from objective facts. Intent is still an element of the offence, so saying it is irrelevant is wrong.

quiz.question: A Doha-based investment firm is licensed in the Qatar Financial Centre. Which statement best describes its AML/CFT regulator?
options: It follows the QCB AML/CFT Instructions like any onshore bank
It has no AML/CFT duties because it is in a financial centre
It is supervised by the QFC Regulatory Authority under the QFC's own rules
It is supervised only by the National Counter Terrorism Committee
quiz.explanation: The QFC has its own regulator, the QFCRA, with its own rulebook. Qatar's AML/CFT law still applies in the country, so the firm certainly has duties; it simply follows a different supervisor's detailed rules.

quiz.question: Under pressure to meet targets, a relationship manager repeatedly ignores missing ownership documents. He says he never intended to help criminals. Why could he still face criminal exposure?
options: Because every missing ownership document is automatically treated as money laundering by the bank
Because relationship managers are personally licensed by the QCB
Because breaching core duties such as CDD through gross negligence is also punishable
Because the bank can transfer all its own liability to the employee
quiz.explanation: The law punishes directors and employees who breach core preventive duties such as CDD wilfully or through gross negligence. Missing documents alone are not laundering, and the bank's own liability remains separate.

quiz.question: A bank asks for a letter of credit for cars priced well below market, shipped from a country different from the beneficiary's. What is this most likely to indicate?
options: A normal discount that needs no further review
Possible trade-based money laundering through under-invoicing
A sanctions breach that must be frozen at once
A customer complaint that belongs with customer service
quiz.explanation: Mispriced goods and odd shipping routes are classic trade-based laundering indicators, as in the QFIU's 2019 car import case. Nothing suggests a listed person, so freezing is not the right first step; escalation to the MLRO is.

sessions.title: Risk Assessment, Customer Due Diligence, Beneficial Owners and PEPs
sessions.summary: Apply the risk-based approach that Law No. 20 of 2019 and the QCB Instructions require: the annual business risk assessment, when and how to carry out CDD, beneficial ownership thresholds, enhanced and simplified measures, and the rules for politically exposed persons.
objectives: Explain the bank's annual ML/TF business risk assessment and the four risk elements used to profile customers
Apply the CDD triggers and steps in the QCB Instructions, including the QR 50,000 one-off threshold
Identify beneficial owners using the 20% ownership and control test and document layered structures
Decide when enhanced or simplified CDD applies and handle PEPs, their family members and close associates

cards.title: A company with a long family tree
cards.setting: Al Wakrah branch, corporate desk, 9:15 am.

lines.text: Big day! A contracting company wants to move its payroll and supplier payments to us. That's a serious relationship for the branch.
Ownership is a bit layered, though: a Qatari company owned by a holding company abroad, which is owned by two individuals and a trust.
And one of the directors shares a family name with an undersecretary at a ministry. Could be a coincidence.
Could be. Our job is to find out, not to guess. Who owns it, who controls it, why they need us, and how risky the relationship is.
The client wants the account open by Thursday.
Then let's work fast and properly. Welcome to the Onboarding Majlis: today you learn to ask the right questions in the right order.

scenes.heading: Know your risks first
scenes.narration: Law Number 20 of 2019 requires banks to identify, assess, document and regularly update their money laundering and terrorist financing risks, and to share the results with the supervisor on request.

scenes.heading: At least once a year
scenes.narration: The QCB Instructions require a business risk assessment at least annually, covering customers, products, delivery channels and technologies, and jurisdictions, and taking the National Risk Assessment into account.

scenes.heading: Before anything new
scenes.narration: New products, business practices and technologies must be risk-assessed before they are launched, not after the first problem appears.

scenes.heading: A board-approved method
scenes.narration: Each bank needs a threat assessment methodology approved by its board, able to score every customer relationship, and the bank must show QCB that practice matches the method.

scenes.heading: Effort follows risk
scenes.narration: The intensity of due diligence and monitoring must match the risk profile: enhanced for higher risk, simplified only where risk is genuinely low and there is no suspicion.

cards.title: The annual risk assessment cycle
cards.caption: The QCB Instructions expect banks to show how they determined their risks, used the National Risk Assessment and whether their actions reduced the risks.

items.label: Identify
items.detail: Customer, product, channel and jurisdiction risks, plus National Risk Assessment findings

items.label: Assess and document
items.detail: Score the risks with the board-approved methodology and record the reasoning

items.label: Mitigate
items.detail: Set policies, controls and monitoring limits that match the risks found

items.label: Monitor
items.detail: Check that controls work in practice, including cash and non-cash limits

items.label: Update
items.detail: Repeat at least once a year and before launching new products or technology

cards.question: How often must a QCB-licensed bank carry out its ML/TF business risk assessment?
options: Only when the QCB announces an inspection
Every three years, with the National Risk Assessment
At regular, appropriate intervals and at least once a year
Only before launching a new product
cards.explanation: The QCB Instructions require the business risk assessment at least once a year. New products need a risk assessment before launch as well, but that is in addition to the annual cycle, not a replacement for it.

cards.title: Customer due diligence step by step
cards.caption: Based on Article 11 of Law No. 20 of 2019 and section 14.3 of the QCB Instructions.

items.label: Identify the customer
items.detail: Collect identification data and the customer's commitment to keep it updated

items.label: Verify identity
items.detail: Use reliable, independent documents, data or information

items.label: Check who acts for whom
items.detail: Establish if the customer acts for another person and verify any agent's authority

items.label: Find the beneficial owner
items.detail: Identify and take reasonable steps to verify the natural persons who own or control

items.label: Understand the purpose
items.detail: Record the purpose and intended nature of the relationship

items.label: Source of wealth and funds
items.detail: Obtain information on where the customer's wealth and funds come from

cards.title: Is CDD required now?
cards.prompt: Under the QCB Instructions, decide whether each event triggers CDD at Dafna Bank.

items.text: A walk-in customer makes a one-off transaction of QR 60,000
Three linked one-off transactions by one person total QR 55,000
A walk-in customer sends a money transfer of QR 4,000
An existing company account adds a new authorised signatory
A QR 900 transaction raises a suspicion of terrorist financing
Staff doubt the passport copy obtained last year is genuine
A long-standing customer's usual monthly salary credit arrives
A customer asks the branch for a printed balance certificate

cards.title: Beneficial owners: the Qatari tests
cards.body:
The beneficial owner is always a **natural person** who ultimately owns or controls the customer, or on whose behalf a transaction is made. The QCB Instructions give practical tests:

- **Companies:** anyone who directly or indirectly owns or controls **at least 20%** of the shares or voting rights, plus anyone who otherwise controls management.
- **Legal arrangements** such as trusts: beneficiaries entitled to at least 20% of the funds, the class of beneficiaries if not yet decided, and anyone controlling at least 20% of the property.
- **Joint stock companies:** also record the names and addresses of shareholders holding **more than 10%** of capital.
- **Layered structures:** obtain and document the ownership and control structure **at every level**.

Verify with reliable, independent sources such as company registers, audited accounts, company searches and bank references. Providing false beneficial ownership information is itself an offence under the law.

cards.title: Onboarding a corporate customer
cards.prompt: Put the steps for opening the contracting company's account in the right order.
steps: Collect the company's identification data, commercial registration and purpose of the relationship
Verify the company's legal status and the authority of the person acting for it
Map the ownership chain at every level down to the natural persons with 20% or more or control
Screen the company, owners and directors, including for PEP status and sanctions lists
Risk-score the relationship using customer, product, channel and jurisdiction factors
Obtain the approvals the risk level requires, such as board or delegated approval after enhanced CDD
Open the account and set the expected activity profile for ongoing monitoring

cards.title: The family name was not a coincidence

lines.text: Screening result is back. The director is the brother of the undersecretary. And the trust's main beneficiary is the undersecretary's daughter.
So we have to say no? The company itself is a genuine contractor.
No. Being a PEP's relative is not a crime and not a reason to refuse by itself. It means the relationship needs enhanced due diligence and the right approval.
Brothers and daughters are family members up to the second degree, so the PEP rules apply to them as if they were the PEP.
Then we need source of wealth, source of funds, and approval from the board or whoever it delegated, before the account opens.
Exactly. Let's make sure everyone in the branch knows the PEP basics.

cards.front: Who is a PEP?
cards.back: Someone who holds or has held a prominent public function in Qatar, in another country or in an international organisation.

cards.front: Who counts as a family member?
cards.back: Relatives by blood or marriage up to the second degree, such as parents, children, siblings, in-laws, step-children and grandchildren.

cards.front: Who is a close associate?
cards.back: A business partner of the PEP, someone linked to the PEP by a business relationship, or a beneficial owner of an entity the PEP controls.

cards.front: Who approves a PEP relationship?
cards.back: The board or the person it delegates, and only after enhanced CDD, including steps to establish source of wealth and funds.

cards.front: What if an existing customer becomes a PEP?
cards.back: The relationship can continue only with the approval of the board or its delegate, followed by enhanced ongoing monitoring.

cards.front: Is hiding PEP status an offence?
cards.back: Yes. Intentionally concealing, or helping to conceal, that a customer is a PEP is a criminal offence under the law.

cards.title: Thursday's deadline
cards.situation: The contracting company's director calls Faisal. He wants the account open today so salaries can be paid on Thursday. Source-of-wealth documents for the PEP-linked trust beneficiary are 'on the way', and the regional manager says approval can be signed 'after the fact'. What should Faisal do?

choices.text: Open the account today and record a note that approval will follow
choices.outcome: This breaks the QCB rule that a PEP relationship may start only after enhanced CDD and approval by the board or its delegate. If problems surface later, the file shows the bank knowingly skipped its own controls.

choices.text: Explain the requirements, complete enhanced CDD quickly and open only after the delegated approval is given
choices.outcome: Right. Speed is fine; skipping steps is not. Faisal can prioritise the file, but the account opens only once EDD is done and the authorised approver signs off.

choices.text: Decline the company permanently because PEP links are too risky
choices.outcome: The bank may decide a relationship is outside its risk appetite, but the rules do not require refusing PEPs. A blanket refusal without assessment can lose good business and is not what the risk-based approach asks for.

cards.title: Simplified versus enhanced CDD
cards.caption: A bank using simplified CDD must keep documentary evidence for why the customer was classed as low risk.

items.label: When used
items.left: Low risk shown by the bank's own and the national risk assessments
items.right: Higher risk, or cases the law, QCB, the committee, the QFIU or FATF calls out

items.label: Examples
items.left: Listed companies on regulated markets; GCC ministries and government bodies
items.right: PEPs, correspondent banks, NPOs, non-residents, private banking, non-face-to-face business

items.label: What changes
items.left: Fewer updates, verification timing may shift
items.right: More information, source of wealth and funds, senior approval, closer monitoring

items.label: Never allowed when
items.left: There is any suspicion of ML/TF or a specific higher-risk scenario
items.right: Not applicable: EDD can always be applied

cards.question: Dafna Bank cannot verify who ultimately owns a company that wants to open an account. What do the law and the QCB Instructions require?
options: Open the account but limit it to incoming payments until ownership is known
Do not open the account, consider an STR and keep a record of the refused customer and the reason
Open the account if a senior manager signs a waiver
Ask the QFIU for permission to open the account
cards.explanation: If CDD cannot be completed, the bank must not open the account or carry out transactions, must consider reporting a suspicion, and the Instructions require separate records of customers refused for this reason. A restricted account still starts a relationship.

cards.title: Enhanced due diligence in practice
cards.prompt: Match each higher-risk situation with a measure the QCB Instructions call for.

pairs.right: Identify the purpose, check the entry visa is valid and keep a copy of the passport
Obtain full details, verify its legal existence and the approval of the competent authority to open the account
Treat both the holder and the grantor as customers and complete CDD on both
Apply enhanced CDD and monitoring, plus countermeasures proportionate to the risk
Seek extra documents, verify them further and confirm identity and address independently

pairs.left: Customer introduced by a third party
pairs.right: Remember the bank stays ultimately responsible for CDD and must hold the CDD records

cards.title: Real case: the nominee owner offer (QFIU, 2019)
cards.body:
In the QFIU's 2019 typologies report, a Qatari real estate agent described an approach from a foreign national.

The man wanted a **well-known Qatari business partner** to be the **registered owner** of land and a housing complex worth millions of US dollars. The partner would keep **10%** as income. The source of the money was never explained, and the agent was offered a **large commission** to make it happen. The agent refused and reported it to the competent authority.

**Why it matters for banks:** this is how beneficial ownership gets hidden. On paper, the respected local partner owns everything; in reality, someone else controls and benefits.

**Lessons for you:**

- Ask who really controls and benefits, not only whose name is on the register.
- An unexplained source of funds plus pressure or unusual rewards is a red flag.
- Nominee arrangements must be identified and documented, and suspicion reported to the MLRO.

cards.title: Real case: the fake charity collector (QFIU, 2019)
cards.body:
Another case in the QFIU's 2019 typologies report came from the non-profit sector.

A man visited gathering places in Qatar, claimed to represent a well-known non-profit organisation and asked crowds for donations. He gave **no official receipts** and had **no collection permit**. The real NPO heard about it and reported him to the Regulatory Authority for Charitable Activities, which alerted law enforcement. Investigators found he had kept the money for himself or passed it to others.

**Why it matters for banks:** NPOs and charitable fundraising are higher-risk areas for both fraud and terrorist financing. That is why the QCB Instructions require **enhanced CDD for NPOs** and full details before any service is offered, and why charitable transfers need the relevant authority's prior approval.

**Lesson:** private accounts that suddenly receive many small 'donations' deserve a closer look.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: Assess ML/TF risks at least yearly with a board-approved method, using the National Risk Assessment, and before launching anything new.
CDD is required for new relationships, one-off or linked transactions of QR 50,000 or more, money transfers above QR 3,500, suspicion and doubts about earlier data.
Beneficial owners are natural persons owning or controlling at least 20%, or controlling otherwise; document every layer.
If CDD cannot be completed: no account, no transaction, consider an STR and keep a record.
PEPs, their family to the second degree and close associates need enhanced CDD and approval from the board or its delegate.

cards.prompt: Think about the last customer you onboarded or reviewed. Could you name every natural person who owns or controls at least 20% of it, and explain where their money comes from?

quiz.question: Which four risk elements must Dafna Bank consider when risk profiling a business relationship under the QCB Instructions?
options: Customer, product or service, interface or delivery channel, and jurisdiction
Customer, staff, branch location and account balance
Product, profit margin, credit score and sector
Nationality, age, income and account type
quiz.explanation: Section 9.3 lists customer risk, product risk, interface or delivery channel risk and jurisdiction risk, plus any other relevant risks. The other options mix in commercial or personal factors that are not the four required elements.

quiz.question: A walk-in customer makes three cash purchases of bank drafts on the same day for QR 18,000, QR 17,000 and QR 16,000. What do the QCB Instructions require?
options: Nothing, because each transaction is below QR 50,000
Only record the transactions, because walk-in customers buying drafts are exempt from CDD under QCB rules
Close the customer's account, because splitting is always illegal
Treat them as linked one-offs of QR 50,000 or more, apply CDD and consider whether they were split
quiz.explanation: CDD applies to a series of linked one-off transactions totalling at least QR 50,000, and the bank must report when it suspects linked transactions are meant to get around that threshold. Walk-in customers are not exempt, and there is no account to close.

quiz.question: Under the QCB Instructions, which individual is a beneficial owner of a company customer?
options: The company's external auditor who signs its accounts
A bank that holds a pledge over the company's shares
A person who indirectly owns 25% of the voting rights through a holding company
A supplier that receives 30% of all of the company's outgoing payments every single month
quiz.explanation: Beneficial ownership covers natural persons who directly or indirectly own or control at least 20% of shares or voting rights, or otherwise control management. Auditors, lenders and suppliers do not own or control the company.

quiz.question: A new corporate customer's ownership runs through three holding companies in two countries. What must the bank do?
options: Record only the immediate shareholder, because foreign holding layers are outside the QCB's scope of review
Obtain and document the ownership and control structure at each level down to the natural persons
Accept a signed statement that no one owns more than 20%
Refuse the customer, because multi-layer structures are prohibited
quiz.explanation: The Instructions require banks to obtain and document the structure at every level of a multi-layered entity. Such structures are not prohibited, but a bare self-declaration cannot replace verification with reliable, independent sources.

quiz.question: Which customer can Dafna Bank potentially treat under simplified CDD, if its risk assessment supports low risk and there is no suspicion?
options: A newly formed trading company with nominee shareholders
A foreign charity collecting cash donations in Qatar
A private banking client introduced by an overseas intermediary that has already completed its own checks
A company listed on a regulated market with disclosure rules meeting international standards
quiz.explanation: The Instructions allow simplified CDD for listed companies on regulated markets with proper disclosure, and for low-risk cases such as certain GCC government bodies. Nominee structures, NPOs and private banking are higher-risk categories that call for enhanced CDD.

quiz.question: An existing customer is appointed as a minister in a neighbouring country. What must the bank do to keep the relationship?
options: Obtain approval from the board or its delegate to continue and apply enhanced ongoing monitoring
Nothing, because PEP rules apply only to new customers
Close the account immediately, because foreign PEPs are not allowed to bank with QCB-licensed institutions
File an STR with the QFIU, because every new PEP must be reported
quiz.explanation: When an existing customer becomes a PEP, the relationship may continue only with board or delegated approval, and PEPs are subject to enhanced ongoing monitoring. PEP status alone is not suspicion, so an automatic STR is wrong.

quiz.question: Which person is a family member of a PEP under the QCB Instructions?
options: The PEP's brother-in-law
The PEP's second cousin
The PEP's former neighbour
The PEP's university classmate
quiz.explanation: Family members are relatives by blood or marriage up to the second degree; the Instructions expressly include brothers- and sisters-in-law. A second cousin is a more distant relative, and neighbours or classmates are not family.

quiz.question: A relationship manager tells a colleague to leave a customer's PEP status out of the file 'so approval is faster'. Which consequence is most serious?
options: It only breaches the bank's customer service standards
Intentionally concealing that a customer is a PEP is a criminal offence under Law No. 20 of 2019
It matters only if the PEP is later convicted of corruption
It is acceptable if the relationship is low value
quiz.explanation: The law makes it an offence to conceal, or help conceal, that a customer is a PEP with unlawful intent. The breach does not depend on value or on any later conviction.

quiz.question: A customer grants his business partner a power of attorney to control his deposit account. Under the QCB Instructions, who must undergo CDD?
options: Only the account holder, because he already has a relationship
Only the attorney holder, because he is the one who will give all the instructions on the account
Neither, if the power of attorney is notarised in Qatar
Both the attorney holder and the grantor, before transactions under the power of attorney
quiz.explanation: Where a power of attorney gives control over the grantor's assets, the holder and the grantor are both treated as customers and CDD is required on both before the bank acts. Notarisation does not replace CDD.

quiz.question: Dafna Bank relies on another regulated bank in its group, abroad, to perform CDD on an introduced customer. Who is responsible if the CDD proves inadequate?
options: The introducing group bank alone, because it performed the CDD
The QCB, because it approves reliance arrangements
Dafna Bank remains ultimately responsible for the CDD measures
The customer, because he supplied the documents
quiz.explanation: Law No. 20 of 2019 allows reliance on third parties but keeps the relying institution ultimately responsible, and the QCB Instructions add that the board remains responsible for proper CDD. The introducer's work does not shift that duty.

sessions.title: Monitoring, Wire Transfers, Correspondent Banking and Sanctions Screening
sessions.summary: Keep watch after onboarding: ongoing monitoring and linked transactions, the QCB rules for wire transfers and money transfers, correspondent and payable-through accounts, shell banks, and screening against UN and National Counter Terrorism Committee lists with action within 24 hours.
objectives: Apply the QCB ongoing monitoring duties, including examining and recording unusual transactions
Handle outgoing and incoming wire transfers with the originator and recipient information Qatar requires
Describe the checks and approvals needed before and during correspondent banking relationships
Act correctly on a confirmed match against UN or NCTC lists, including the 24-hour steps

cards.title: Three alerts before coffee
cards.setting: Transaction monitoring room, Dafna Bank head office. 7:50 am.

lines.text: Morning, everyone. Three things overnight. First: a customer made cash deposits at ATMs after 10 pm, and within an hour the money was withdrawn by card abroad.
Second is mine. An incoming SWIFT transfer from a bank overseas, no originator address, no account number. Just a name.
And third: a bank in a high-risk jurisdiction wants us to open a correspondent account for them. Their sales pitch is very polished.
Monitoring, wires and correspondents in one morning. That's the Corniche Wire Room for you: money moving in every direction.
And our screening system has a possible name match on one of the beneficiaries, so sanctions too.
Then let's take them one by one. By the end of this stage you'll know exactly what Qatar's rules expect at each step.

scenes.heading: Compare against the profile
scenes.narration: For every customer, the bank must check that transactions match what it knows about the customer, the business, the risk profile and, where needed, the source of funds and wealth.

scenes.heading: Keep files fresh
scenes.narration: Customer documents and data must be reviewed and kept up to date, with particular attention to higher-risk customers.

scenes.heading: Unusual deserves a look
scenes.narration: Complex, unusually large or oddly patterned transactions with no clear economic or lawful purpose must be examined, and the findings written down and kept.

scenes.heading: Real-time ability
scenes.narration: The QCB Instructions expect monitoring systems that can review transactions in real time and flag them for further examination.

scenes.heading: Join the dots
scenes.narration: Systems must link one-off transactions to the same person, so that splitting a large amount into smaller pieces does not slip through.

cards.title: From alert to decision
cards.caption: Unusual is not the same as suspicious. The QCB Instructions require you to examine and record; suspicion then goes to the MLRO without delay.

items.label: Alert or observation
items.detail: Generated by the monitoring system or noticed by staff

items.label: Compare with the profile
items.detail: Expected activity, business, risk rating, source of funds

items.label: Examine and record
items.detail: Background and purpose of the transaction, documented on file

items.label: Decide
items.detail: Explained and closed, or suspicion reported to the MLRO

cards.title: Real case: night-time ATM deposits (QFIU, 2019)
cards.body:
A Qatari bank presented this pattern at the QFIU's 2019 typologies workshop.

A customer **only** used ATMs to deposit cash, typically **after 10 pm**, in odd amounts just **below the daily ATM limit**, and never visited a branch. Within about **an hour**, the **entire amount** was withdrawn by card from ATMs in a **high-risk jurisdiction**, using a supplementary card.

**Why it matters:** each deposit looked small and harmless. The pattern showed someone avoiding staff contact and moving cash abroad quickly, which can point to laundering or terrorist financing.

**Lessons for you:**

- Monitoring must link activity over time and across channels.
- Avoiding face-to-face contact is itself an indicator.
- Fast in-and-out movement to high-risk places should be examined, recorded and escalated.

cards.question: A customer's monthly turnover suddenly triples. The monitoring team finds no obvious reason. What do the QCB Instructions say comes next?
options: Examine the background and purpose, record the findings and report to the MLRO if suspicion arises
File an STR straight away, because any unusual activity is suspicious
Ignore it, because the customer already passed CDD at onboarding
Close the account without telling anyone why
cards.explanation: The Instructions say an unusual or inconsistent transaction is not suspicious by itself; it must be examined and the findings recorded. If knowledge or suspicion results, it goes to the MLRO. Ignoring it or closing the account without review skips the required steps.

cards.title: Wire transfer information under the QCB Instructions
cards.caption: Full originator information includes name, account number or unique reference and details such as address, ID number or date and place of birth, plus purpose and relationship to the beneficiary.

items.label: When it applies
items.left: Ordering bank in Qatar, beneficiary bank or agent abroad
items.right: Ordering and beneficiary institutions and all customers in Qatar

items.label: What travels with the payment
items.left: Full originator and full recipient information
items.right: All information, but below QR 3,500 the names and account numbers or a unique reference may suffice

items.label: Condition for the reduced set
items.right: Full details given to the beneficiary bank, QCB or QFIU within three days of request, and to law enforcement immediately

items.label: Always
items.left: No transfer of any value with UN- or NCTC-listed persons
items.right: No transfer of any value with UN- or NCTC-listed persons

cards.title: An incoming transfer with missing details
cards.prompt: Samuel's team receives a transfer for a Dafna customer with no originator account number or address. Put the steps in order.
steps: Detect that required originator information is missing or incomplete
Decide under the bank's risk-based policy whether to reject the transfer or request the missing data
Ask the ordering bank for the missing originator information
Consider, on a risk-sensitive basis, whether the gap or the reply gives grounds for an STR
Record the case and keep the information received for at least 10 years
If the same ordering bank keeps failing, warn it, set deadlines and restrict or end the relationship

cards.question: A Dafna customer collects an incoming money transfer of QR 5,000 at a branch. The recipient has never been identified by the bank before. What must the bank do before paying?
options: Pay out, because only outgoing transfers need checks
Pay out, because identification applies only above QR 50,000
Ask the ordering bank to verify the recipient on its behalf
Verify the recipient's identity, because the amount is above QR 3,500
cards.explanation: For transfers above QR 3,500 the beneficiary institution must verify the recipient's identity before making the money available, unless it was verified before. The QR 50,000 figure is the threshold for one-off transactions, not for paying out transfers.

cards.title: A polished pitch from far away

lines.text: The respondent bank is licensed in a jurisdiction on FATF's list of strategic deficiencies. They want a US dollar account and say their customers will 'use it directly'.
Use it directly? That sounds like a payable-through account.
Their questionnaire is glossy, but the ownership section says 'available on request'.
Before any correspondent relationship, Qatar's rules expect us to understand their business, ownership, management, supervision and AML controls, and the board must approve it.
And if their customers will touch our account directly, we must be sure the respondent has done CDD on them and can show it to us on request.
So: no shortcuts, a signed agreement, and an annual review if we go ahead. Let me build the checklist.

cards.front: Is a shell bank allowed?
cards.back: No. Banks must not start or continue relationships with shell banks, and must report to the QFIU if approached by one.

cards.front: What about respondents serving shell banks?
cards.back: Not allowed. The respondent must not let shell banks use its accounts.

cards.front: Who approves a new correspondent relationship?
cards.back: The board of directors, after the due diligence checks are completed.

cards.front: What must be signed?
cards.back: An agreement setting out each bank's AML/CFT responsibilities for detection and monitoring.

cards.front: Respondent in a high-risk jurisdiction?
cards.back: Apply enhanced ongoing monitoring of the transactions and review the relationship every year.

cards.front: What should you check about the respondent?
cards.back: Reputation, supervision, ownership and management, AML/CFT controls, any ML/TF investigations and whether its leaders are on sanctions lists.

cards.title: The respondent that went quiet
cards.situation: Dafna Bank has a correspondent relationship with a foreign bank whose customers can use Dafna's account directly. Samuel notices a series of large payments by one of the respondent's customers to a trading company with no visible link to its business. He asks the respondent for that customer's CDD documents. Two weeks and two reminders later, there is no reply. What should he do?

choices.text: Keep waiting, because the respondent is a long-standing partner
choices.outcome: Waiting lets unexplained payments continue through Dafna's account. The QCB Instructions set a clear consequence when a respondent fails to provide requested CDD information.

choices.text: Terminate that customer's direct access to the account and consider an STR with the MLRO
choices.outcome: Right. For payable-through access, if the respondent fails to provide the requested CDD information, the correspondent must cut off the customer's access and consider reporting to the QFIU.

choices.text: Close the entire correspondent relationship at once without further steps
choices.outcome: Ending the relationship may become necessary, but it skips the specific steps: stop that customer's access and consider an STR. Closing everything abruptly without recording the reasons or escalating also misses the suspicion question.

cards.title: Sanctions screening and targeted financial sanctions
cards.body:
Law No. 20 of 2019 requires banks to have systems to comply with **targeted financial sanctions**, and it prohibits wire transfers with persons and entities listed under UN Security Council resolutions. The wider regime is set by **Law No. 27 of 2019 on Combating Terrorism** and a 2020 implementing decision, with designations circulated by the **National Counter Terrorism Committee (NCTC)**.

The QCB Instructions (section 10.4) turn this into a bank duty:

- **Screen** customers and parties from the start of dealings and **throughout** the relationship against UN Security Council lists and terrorist designation orders circulated by the NCTC.
- On a confirmed match: **do not establish or continue** the relationship or carry out the transaction, **immediately (within 24 hours)**.
- **File an STR** with the QFIU.
- **Inform the QCB** immediately (within 24 hours).

The exact freezing procedures are set by the national TFS authorities; follow your bank's sanctions procedure and the official notices.

cards.title: Confirmed sanctions match: do or don't?
cards.prompt: Anjali confirms that a beneficiary is on an NCTC-circulated designation. Sort the actions.

items.text: Stop the transaction and any dealing within 24 hours
Escalate to the MLRO so an STR is filed with the QFIU
Inform the QCB within 24 hours
Record the screening result and every action taken
Tell the customer the payment is blocked because of a sanctions list
Release the payment because the amount is small
Wait for the next monthly screening cycle to confirm
Ask the customer to resend the payment to a different beneficiary

cards.title: A confirmed match: the first 24 hours
cards.caption: Based on section 10.4 of the QCB AML/CFT Instructions. Follow any freezing instructions from the competent national authorities.

items.label: Confirm the match
items.detail: Rule out false positives using identifiers such as date of birth and nationality

items.label: Stop
items.detail: Do not process the transaction or continue the relationship

items.label: Escalate
items.detail: Alert the MLRO at once; the MLRO files an STR with the QFIU

items.label: Notify QCB
items.detail: Inform the Qatar Central Bank within 24 hours

items.label: Protect and record
items.detail: Keep the matter confidential and document every step

cards.title: Real case: donations that never left (QFIU, 2019)
cards.body:
At the QFIU's 2019 typologies workshop, a Qatari bank described a terrorist financing attempt it stopped.

A customer received **many small local credits** from different people through standing orders and transfers. He then **consolidated** them and tried to send a **foreign transfer** to an educational institution in a South Asian country. The bank's **screening system flagged negative news**: the institution had hosted speakers blacklisted for hate speech and recruitment for a terrorist organisation. The bank **rejected the transaction**.

**Indicators the bank saw:** many small payments into one account, funds pooled for an unregistered charitable purpose, a transfer to a foreign organisation, and a beneficiary linked to terrorism in open sources.

**Lesson:** screening is more than list matching. Adverse media and the shape of the money flow together exposed the risk.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: Monitor every relationship against the customer's profile, examine unusual transactions and record your findings.
Cross-border wires need full originator and recipient information; a beneficiary bank must reject or chase missing data and consider an STR.
Verify the recipient before paying out transfers above QR 3,500, and keep wire information for at least 10 years.
Correspondent relationships need full due diligence, board approval and a signed agreement; shell banks are prohibited.
On a UN or NCTC list match: stop within 24 hours, file an STR through the MLRO and inform the QCB within 24 hours.

cards.prompt: Where in your role could money move without anyone comparing it to the customer's profile? Name one check you could add or strengthen.

quiz.question: Under the QCB Instructions, what must a bank do when it notices a complex, unusually large transaction with no apparent economic purpose?
options: Reverse the transaction and refund the customer
File an STR automatically without any review
Examine its background and purpose and record the findings
Note it only if the amount exceeds QR 50,000
quiz.explanation: The Instructions require banks to pay particular attention to such transactions, examine their background and purpose and keep a record. Unusual is not automatically suspicious, and no amount threshold applies.

quiz.question: Dafna Bank in Doha sends a customer's payment to a bank in Europe. What information must accompany the transfer?
options: Only the originator's name, because the amount is small
Full originator information and full recipient information
Only the recipient's account number
Whatever the recipient bank asks for after the payment arrives
quiz.explanation: When the ordering institution is in Qatar and the beneficiary institution or agent is abroad, full originator and full recipient information must travel with the transfer. The reduced data set applies only to certain domestic transfers below QR 3,500.

quiz.question: An incoming cross-border transfer for a Dafna customer arrives without the originator's account number or address. What must Dafna, as the beneficiary bank in Qatar, do?
options: Reject it or obtain the missing information, and decide on a risk basis whether to report it
Credit the customer and treat the gap as the ordering bank's problem
Return it automatically and close the customer's account
Credit the customer and complete the missing originator details from its own records of earlier payments
quiz.explanation: The Instructions require the beneficiary institution to reject the transfer or get the missing information from the ordering institution, and to decide on a risk-sensitive basis whether an STR is needed. Ignoring the gap or inventing data is not acceptable.

quiz.question: One foreign ordering bank keeps sending transfers to Dafna without originator details. What do the QCB Instructions expect?
options: Accept the transfers, because repeated gaps from one bank show a technical issue rather than a money laundering risk to report
Inform the customer that the ordering bank is under review
Ask the QCB to fine the ordering bank directly
Warn it, set deadlines, reject transfers or restrict the relationship, and report to the QFIU when appropriate
quiz.explanation: When an ordering institution regularly fails to provide required information, the beneficiary must act, for example by warning, setting deadlines, rejecting transfers or restricting or ending the relationship, and report to the QFIU when appropriate. Telling the customer risks tipping off.

quiz.question: Which relationship is Dafna Bank prohibited from entering into under Law No. 20 of 2019?
options: A correspondent relationship with a bank that has no physical presence or regulated group
A correspondent relationship with a bank in another GCC country
A correspondent relationship with a bank that has a parent company abroad
A correspondent relationship with a bank supervised by its home central bank in a country outside the GCC
quiz.explanation: Relationships with shell banks, which have no meaningful physical presence and no affiliation to a supervised group, are prohibited. The other options describe ordinary, supervised banks that still require due diligence but are not banned.

quiz.question: Samuel completes due diligence on a new respondent bank. Who must approve the new correspondent relationship under the QCB Instructions?
options: The head of the trade finance desk
The board of directors
The respondent bank's compliance officer
The QFIU
quiz.explanation: Section 11.4 requires board approval before a correspondent banking relationship is established. Desk heads and the respondent's own officers cannot approve on Dafna's behalf, and the QFIU does not approve relationships.

quiz.question: A respondent bank operates in a high-risk jurisdiction. Besides the standard checks, what do the QCB Instructions require?
options: A review every five years, as for other respondents
Monthly approval of each transaction by the QFIU
No extra measures if the respondent is profitable
Enhanced ongoing monitoring of its transactions and an annual review of the relationship
quiz.explanation: For a respondent in a high-risk jurisdiction, the correspondent must apply enhanced ongoing monitoring and review the relationship annually. The QFIU does not approve transactions, and profitability is irrelevant to the requirement.

quiz.question: Anjali confirms that a customer is named in a terrorist designation circulated by the National Counter Terrorism Committee. Which set of actions matches the QCB Instructions?
options: Continue normal service while the match is reviewed and inform the QCB at the next quarterly supervisory meeting
Tell the customer about the listing so he can appeal quickly
Stop dealing within 24 hours, have the MLRO file an STR and inform the QCB within 24 hours
Wait for the UN to add the same name before acting
quiz.explanation: Section 10.4 requires the bank not to establish or continue the relationship or carry out transactions, immediately and within 24 hours, to make an STR to the QFIU and to inform the QCB within 24 hours. NCTC-circulated designations are acted on directly, and telling the customer is not part of the process.

quiz.question: A walk-in customer asks the branch to send QR 2,000 to a charity abroad through the bank. What should staff check first under the QCB Instructions?
options: Nothing, because the amount is below QR 3,500
Only that the charity has a website
Whether the customer will donate again next month
Whether the required prior approval from the relevant authority for charitable transfers has been obtained
quiz.explanation: The Instructions prohibit transfers of any value for charitable causes through banks or money transfer providers without prior approval from the relevant authority and completion of its requirements. The QR 3,500 figure concerns wire information and identification, not charity approvals.

quiz.question: A customer makes cash ATM deposits late at night just below the daily limit, and the whole amount is withdrawn abroad within an hour in a high-risk country. What is the best response?
options: Ignore it, because each individual deposit is below the ATM limit and no single amount looks unusual
Block the customer's card and tell him why
Treat it as a pattern to examine and record, and escalate any suspicion to the MLRO
Increase his ATM limit so he can use the branch less
quiz.explanation: This mirrors a case from the QFIU's 2019 typologies report: deposits below limits, avoidance of staff and fast withdrawal in a high-risk place. Individual amounts do not matter; the pattern must be examined and suspicion escalated, without tipping off the customer.

sessions.title: Reporting Suspicion to the QFIU and Avoiding Tipping Off
sessions.summary: Turn a concern into a report that works: internal STRs to the MLRO, the MLRO's duties, the QFIU's April 2024 reporting instructions and deadlines, what a strong STR narrative contains, protection for good-faith reporting, and how to avoid tipping off.
objectives: Make a prompt internal STR to the MLRO and describe what the MLRO must do on receiving it
Apply the QFIU deadlines of 24 hours and three working days and the rules on who may file
Write or support an STR narrative that meets the QFIU's quality expectations
Recognise tipping off and handle CDD, restrictions and customer questions without alerting the customer

cards.title: Why so many questions?
cards.setting: Al Wakrah branch, money transfer counter, 4:15 pm, Wednesday.

lines.text: Noora, my teller Reem has a regular customer, a young man, who sends small transfers to the same few accounts abroad. Always 'family maintenance', always for different drivers and maids.
Today he asked to send a larger amount and refused to say who the beneficiary was. When Reem asked, he cancelled and left.
So the transaction didn't happen. Does that mean there's nothing to report?
Attempted transactions count. The law requires reporting of suspicious transactions including attempted ones, whatever the amount.
He also asked Reem, 'Why so many questions? Are you reporting me?' She didn't know what to say.
Then today we climb the Signal Tower: how to report, how fast, and how to stay silent about it.

cards.title: Two steps from suspicion to the QFIU

scenes.heading: Step one: tell the MLRO
scenes.narration: Every officer and employee must make an internal suspicious transaction report to the MLRO promptly, whatever the amount, and keep passing on later transactions the MLRO asks for.

scenes.heading: The MLRO decides
scenes.narration: The MLRO documents the report, acknowledges it in writing with a reminder about tipping off, reviews all the bank's information, decides, and tells the reporter in writing.

scenes.heading: Step two: report to the QFIU
scenes.narration: If there are grounds to suspect, the MLRO or Deputy MLRO files the STR with the QFIU, normally through its electronic E-STR system.

scenes.heading: Clock and consultation
scenes.narration: The QFIU's 2024 instructions set outer time limits, and the QCB Instructions say related transactions must not proceed without consulting the QFIU.

scenes.heading: Protected, but silent
scenes.narration: Staff who report in good faith are protected from liability, but no one may reveal that a report has been made or is being considered.

cards.title: What the MLRO does with an internal STR
cards.caption: Based on sections 19.3 and 19.9 of the QCB AML/CFT Instructions.

items.label: Document it
items.detail: If it was raised orally, record it properly

items.label: Acknowledge in writing
items.detail: Confirm receipt to the reporter, with a reminder about tipping off

items.label: Review everything
items.detail: Consider all information the bank holds on the customer and transaction

items.label: Decide
items.detail: Is the transaction suspicious? Act independently and honestly

items.label: Notify the reporter
items.detail: Give written notice of the decision

items.label: Keep records
items.detail: Details of the internal STR, the review and any STR to the QFIU

cards.title: Indicator or not enough on its own?
cards.prompt: Section 19.1 of the QCB Instructions lists factors that help decide if a transaction is suspicious. Sort each observation.

items.text: No apparent economic or lawful purpose
Customer fails to give an adequate explanation when asked
Funds routed through third parties for no clear reason
Offshore companies not supported by the customer's needs
Size or pattern unlike the customer's past activity, with no explanation
The customer is a foreign national
The transaction is large but matches the customer's known business
The customer's account is new, with activity fully in line with its stated purpose

cards.question: Who may file Dafna Bank's suspicious transaction reports with the QFIU?
options: Any employee who first noticed the suspicion
The MLRO or the Deputy MLRO registered with the QFIU
The branch manager of the branch involved
The head of internal audit
cards.explanation: The QCB Instructions say the STR must be made by the MLRO or Deputy MLRO, and the QFIU's 2024 instructions accept STRs only from approved, registered reporting officers. Other staff report internally to the MLRO.

cards.title: The QFIU reporting clock (April 2024 instructions)
cards.caption: These are outer limits. The law asks for prompt reporting and the QCB Instructions say 'immediately'. The suspicion date must be stated in the report.

items.label: Suspicion determined
items.detail: The bank decides, under its internal procedures, that there are grounds to suspect

items.label: Terrorism or high-risk crime
items.detail: Deadline when linked to a terrorist, terrorist act or organisation, or to high-risk crimes in the National Risk Assessment

items.label: All other STRs
items.detail: Outer limit for other suspicions; Fridays, Saturdays and official holidays are not counted

items.label: Fixing a returned STR
items.detail: Time to send extra information or a revised STR after a QFIU notice, or it may be rejected

cards.title: What a strong STR narrative contains

lines.text: I've looked at Faisal's customer. Twelve senders over three months, all small amounts, all to the same three accounts in one country. Different 'drivers' and 'maids' each time.
And the big transfer yesterday never went through.
The QFIU's instructions say reports cover attempted transactions too, including when a customer walks away after being asked about the beneficiary.
The pattern looks like a case in the QFIU's typologies report: small remittances, third-party senders, structured amounts.
Then I'll file. Today, so we're well inside the three working days. Faisal, the next question is what Reem says if he comes back.

cards.title: The customer comes back
cards.situation: The next morning the young man returns to Reem's counter. 'My transfer is blocked, isn't it? Did you report me to the police?' A queue is forming behind him. What should Reem say?

choices.text: 'Yes, our compliance team has sent a report, so I can't help you.'
choices.outcome: This is tipping off: it reveals that an STR has been made. Disclosing that a report has been filed with the QFIU is a criminal offence under Law No. 20 of 2019, and it may let the customer move funds or destroy evidence.

choices.text: 'I'm not able to process this today. Let me take your details and someone will contact you.' Then she informs the MLRO.
choices.outcome: Right. Reem stays neutral, gives no hint of a report, does not invent false accusations, and lets the MLRO decide on any next contact. The MLRO can also record the customer's question.

choices.text: 'There's no problem at all, please try again tomorrow.'
choices.outcome: It avoids naming the report but misleads the customer and may encourage a new attempt the bank is not ready for. A neutral answer and immediate escalation to the MLRO are safer.

cards.front: What is tipping off?
cards.back: Disclosing that an STR has been or may be made, or that an ML/TF investigation is under way, in a way that could harm prevention or detection.

cards.front: Who can be told about an internal STR?
cards.back: Only the board, or others with the MLRO's consent; the MLRO consents only if disclosure would not tip off and records it.

cards.front: What if CDD would tip off the customer?
cards.back: Do not pursue the CDD; file an STR instead. The MLRO must record the grounds for that belief.

cards.front: Can the bank end the relationship after an STR?
cards.back: Yes, for normal commercial reasons, but without tipping off, and the bank must inform the QCB immediately.

cards.front: Is good-faith reporting protected?
cards.back: Yes. Reporters are protected from criminal and civil liability, even if they did not know the exact offence or it never happened.

cards.front: Can information go to group branches abroad?
cards.back: The law's ban on disclosure does not stop information sharing with foreign branches and majority-owned subsidiaries.

cards.title: STR situations and the right handling
cards.prompt: Match each situation with what the law, the QCB Instructions or the QFIU instructions require.

pairs.left: Customer walks away when asked who the beneficiary is
pairs.right: Report the attempted transaction; attempts count, whatever the amount
Report anyway; STRs are required whether or not tax matters are involved

pairs.left: STR made about a proposed transaction
pairs.right: Inform the QCB, and do not let the transaction proceed without consulting the QFIU

pairs.left: Customer under investigation after an STR
pairs.right: Do not destroy any customer records without consulting the QFIU

pairs.left: New suspicion about a person already reported
pairs.right: File a linked STR, cite the earlier reference and restate the earlier grounds

pairs.left: Urgent case needing postponement or freezing
pairs.right: File and contact the QFIU Analysis Department to flag the urgency

cards.question: Dafna Bank determines on a Thursday that a transaction is suspected of involving fraud proceeds. Nothing links it to terrorism or high-risk crimes. Under the QFIU's 2024 instructions, what is the latest the STR may be filed?
options: By Friday, within 24 hours
By the following Sunday, three calendar days later
By the following Tuesday, three working days later, as Friday and Saturday are not counted
Within 30 days, at the next monthly reporting cycle
cards.explanation: Other suspicions must be reported within three working days of determination, excluding Fridays, Saturdays and official holidays: Sunday, Monday and Tuesday. The 24-hour limit applies to terrorism-linked or high-risk crime cases, and prompt reporting is still expected.

cards.title: Real case: small remittances, big pattern (QFIU, 2019)
cards.body:
Exchange houses shared this case at the QFIU's 2019 typologies workshop.

Customers aged roughly **19 to 35** sent **small remittances**, usually under **QR 500**, to South Asian countries known for drug trafficking. They said it was **family maintenance** for domestic workers or drivers. Reviews showed **many senders paying the same beneficiaries**, beneficiaries with **multiple accounts**, and third parties of the beneficiary's nationality used as senders. Follow-up with the QFIU and the Ministry of Interior found most of the money was paying for **drugs**.

**Lessons for you:**

- Small amounts do not mean low risk; there is no threshold for suspicion.
- Look across customers: shared beneficiaries reveal networks.
- Stated purposes must make sense for the customer's own life and relationships.

cards.title: How the QFIU handled reports in 2022
cards.caption: Source: QFIU Annual Report 2021-2022. A clear, complete narrative helps the QFIU prioritise and act on your report.

items.label: STRs from financial institutions
items.detail: Out of 1,403 reports received in 2022

items.label: Rated high priority
items.detail: Using criteria linked to the National Risk Assessment

items.label: Rated medium priority
items.detail: Also analysed; low-priority data is stored and can trigger alerts later

items.label: Disseminated
items.detail: Share passed to competent authorities after analysis

cards.title: Writing for the QFIU
cards.body:
- **Write for a stranger.** The analyst does not know your systems; avoid internal codes and abbreviations.
- **Tell it in order.** Dates, amounts and accounts in chronological sequence.
- **Show your reasoning.** Normal behaviour, what changed, why it matters.
- **Attach the evidence.** Verified ID data and transaction records, kept as complete and current as possible.
- **Watch the clock.** Record the suspicion date in the report.
- **Stay silent.** Never hint to the customer or colleagues outside the need-to-know circle.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: Every employee must report suspicion to the MLRO promptly, whatever the amount, including attempted transactions.
Only the registered MLRO or Deputy MLRO files STRs with the QFIU, normally through the E-STR system.
Outer limits: 24 hours for terrorism-linked or high-risk crime cases, three working days for others, excluding Fridays, Saturdays and official holidays.
A strong STR explains normal versus unusual behaviour, people and links, a dated sequence and the suspicion date, without jargon.
Tipping off is a crime; good-faith reporting is protected. If CDD would tip off, file an STR instead.

cards.prompt: Imagine a customer asks you directly whether you have reported them. Write down, in one or two sentences, the neutral answer you would give and who you would tell next.

quiz.question: A teller suspects a QR 700 transfer may be linked to terrorist financing. Under the QCB Instructions, what must she do?
options: Wait until the customer's transfers exceed QR 3,500
Make an internal STR to the MLRO immediately, regardless of the amount
Report directly to the QFIU from her own email
Ask the customer to explain the purpose in writing first
quiz.explanation: Internal STRs must be made promptly to the MLRO irrespective of amount, and only the MLRO or Deputy files with the QFIU. Asking the customer to justify himself in writing risks tipping off.

quiz.question: After receiving an internal STR, which step must the MLRO take under the QCB Instructions?
options: Give the reporter a written acknowledgment with a reminder about tipping off
Inform the customer that a review is under way
Forward the report unchanged to the QFIU within one hour, without adding the bank's own review
Pass the report to the branch manager for a decision
quiz.explanation: The MLRO must document the report, acknowledge it in writing with a tipping-off reminder, consider all relevant information, decide whether it is suspicious and tell the reporter in writing. Forwarding without review skips the MLRO's own assessment.
